sections.h2: Who bills and collects property tax in Ann Arbor
sections.html:
Ann Arbor collects its own property tax through the city Treasury unit, and the city Assessor sets the values behind each bill. If real property tax stays unpaid past winter, the account moves to Washtenaw County.

Property tax is more than half of the city's revenue, so assessments get close attention. Your bill is a combined figure: the city levy plus the county, the schools and other taxing units, each with its own millage.

A separate administration fee also appears. State law lets the city add up to 1 percent of the tax, and the money offsets the cost of defending assessments and collecting for every taxing unit.

Two bills arrive each year. Summer tax is billed July 1 and winter tax December 1, and the last penalty-free days fall at the end of those months. County operating tax rides on the summer bill, and the voted county millages ride on the winter one.

Missing the winter deadline starts a short countdown. Real property tax still unpaid on February 28 goes to the Washtenaw County Treasurer, and extra penalties and interest begin March 1. After that handoff the city can no longer show the account, so call the county to find out whether a late balance has been paid.

The formula is simple. Take the taxable value, divide by 1,000, multiply by the millage rate, then multiply by 1.01 for the fee. Taxable value often trails assessed value because Proposal A, passed by Michigan voters in 1994, ties its yearly growth to the smaller of 5 percent or inflation, with additions counted separately. Assessed value itself targets half of market value.

The city's online estimator shows annual millage totals of 52.8802 for principal residences and 68.8196 for other property. Rates change from year to year, and your parcel's actual bill depends on the units that cover it.

Your taxable value is printed on the annual bill and on the assessment notice, which the city mails around the first week of March. The online property record card holds the figures behind both.

sections.h2: Why the bill jumps after a sale
sections.html:
After a sale or transfer, the next tax year's taxable value is set equal to the assessed value, the half-of-market figure. Ann Arbor calls that uncapping. The yearly limit then applies again until ownership changes once more.

That rule is why a buyer's first full bill can top the one you paid. A long-held house may carry a taxable value well under its assessed value, and the buyer starts without that cushion. With homes valued at a median of $453,400, the difference can be sizable. Buyers often ask about it, so expect the question at showings.

The Assessor's Office, on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, takes the Property Transfer Affidavit, the Principal Residence Exemption affidavit and the request to rescind that exemption. Hand them in, submit them on the online forms page or mail them. Questions go to 734.794.6530 or assessor@a2gov.org.

Start with the city Board of Review, which sits four days beginning the Monday of March's third week. You appear by appointment, and the Assessor hands out the appeal forms. Board members are appointed citizens, approved by council, and do not work for the city.

The case that works shows assessed value running past 50 percent of true cash value. Complaining that taxes keep climbing does not count, because taxable value may rise yearly by inflation or 5 percent, whichever is lower. Useful evidence includes comparable nearby sales, mistakes on your record card and a repair estimate for something like a leaking basement.

  • A homeowner has to protest at the local board before taking a case to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • The Tribunal filing date is July 31 for homes, and May 31 for commercial and industrial real property and business personal property.
  • The board mails its decision some weeks after it adjourns, along with the next appeal steps.

Certain owners can put off the summer bill: senior citizens, people with qualifying disabilities or blindness, and eligible service members and their surviving spouses. A summer deferment carries a $40,000 household income cap. Pick up the application at the Customer Service Center, 301 E. Huron St., or find it at washtenaw.org, and file it with the treasurer by September 15.

Real property balances that moved to the county are handled by the Washtenaw County Treasurer at 734.222.6600 or taxes@washtenaw.org. Overdue personal property tax stays with the city, and 734.994.2833 gives the amount.

If you plan to sell with a bill outstanding, request the figures before you list. The closing agent pays what is owed from your proceeds, so a clear number early keeps the settlement statement from surprising you. Ask for the figure in writing if you can, and note which taxing unit holds the balance, since the city and the county answer for different accounts.

A practical order of steps: ask the city Treasury for the current balance, and the county if anything went past February 28. Gather your Property Transfer Affidavit and, if it applies, the request to rescind your Principal Residence Exemption. Then give the closing agent both numbers so the payoff is built into the closing.

A cash sale does not change what the tax bill says, but it can skip the repair negotiations and lender appraisal that slow a conventional closing.

sections.h2: Ann Arbor housing at a glance
sections.html: The estimated 2025 population is 122,233. Owners hold 45.5 percent of 50,499 households, so renters are the majority, and many sellers here are landlords or heirs with an older house. The typical home value is $453,400 and typical gross rent is $1,649. Monthly owner costs at the midpoint run $2,436 with a mortgage and $1,036 without. When repairs stand in the way of a conventional sale, a buyer who takes the property as-is can close without them.

faqs.q: What is the due date for Ann Arbor summer tax?
faqs.a: July 31, with payments accepted from July 1. Winter tax runs on the same pattern, opening December 1 and closing December 31.

faqs.q: Where can I pay my Ann Arbor tax in person?
faqs.a: Use the Customer Service and Payment Center inside Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A drive-up drop box at East Ann Street and North Fifth Avenue stays open around the clock.

faqs.q: Does selling change an Ann Arbor taxable value?
faqs.a: Yes, for the buyer. The year after a transfer, taxable value is reset to the assessed value, a step the city calls uncapping.

faqs.q: When must an Ann Arbor homeowner file with the Michigan Tax Tribunal?
faqs.a: By July 31, after first protesting at the March Board of Review. Commercial and industrial real property and business personal property must file by May 31.

faqs.q: Who collects Ann Arbor real property tax that is still unpaid in March?
faqs.a: The Washtenaw County Treasurer, at 734.222.6600, takes real property tax not received by February 28. Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city.
